prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms enabled atomic frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock (B024) as my single preferred part after the full first-round exchange. The reasons are unchanged and I think they have survived the objections. The central idea is Katori's magic-wavelength lattice: a trapping wavelength at which the light shift on the clock transition cancels to first order, so that very many neutral atoms are confined in the Lamb-Dicke regime, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and probed together. As a theorist who computes polarizabilities and magic wavelengths for a living I can say this is not a refinement of the single-ion approach honoured in 2012, because the error budget and the statistics are of a different kind. Ye's strontium clocks, and the intercomparisons between laboratories, then demonstrated what the idea buys: stability and systematic uncertainty near 1e-18, reproduced independently in many national institutes. The credited pair maps exactly onto invention and realisation with nobody forced out by the three-person limit, which is the property that no other shortlisted candidate shares. The chair's summary confirms that nobody calls B024 scientifically premature or unconfirmed; the disagreement is about lineage, not about the soundness of the result. I would keep the citation anchored on invention and realisation, and not on discoveries made with the clocks, because those are so far limits and capability rather than findings.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against is the lineage worry: the 2005 prize (comb) and the 2012 prize (single-ion control) already covered the precision-measurement thread, and a committee that wants a prize about a new phenomenon in nature would look at B044 first. I have tested that objection and I still think the clock is a different physical idea, but I accept that a reasonable member can weigh it differently, and that the payoff in fundamental physics (the redefinition of the second, constants, dark matter, geodesy) is still partly prospective. Second, a two-name credit invites the question of Yb and Hg lattice work, Al+ ion clocks and the Sr groups who will ask why the prize is not broader; I think the invention-and-realisation citation answers it but not completely. Third, I should recognise that B044 has broader opening support (six rankers, four in the top three) than B024 (five rankers), and my loyalty to B024 may carry a specialist's bias towards atomic measurement. I do not treat support counts as a scientific argument, but I do not want to ignore that several members from far-apart fields converge on B044.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B044 first as a new phase of matter, a symmetry-protected Z2 insulator distinct from what Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were honoured for in 2016, and places it above a metrological improvement.
responses.response: On the 2016 overlap I have to revise my own first-round wording, which the chair has asked about. For time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulators specifically I accept that Danielsson, Eriksson and Olsson are right: the 2016 prize concerned topological phase transitions and Chern-type quantum Hall topology, and a symmetry-protected state without a magnetic field is a different class, so I no longer count the overlap as reducing novelty. What I do not accept is that this makes B044 ready. My remaining objection is attribution, not novelty: the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang that told Molenkamp what to measure sits outside the supplied names, and so does the three-dimensional work. A narrower citation can limit the claim to the prediction and the two-dimensional HgTe discovery, but then the prize is about a smaller thing than the field Danielsson wants to honour. I therefore keep B044 as my first alternative and would not oppose it if the committee's weighing comes out the other way. What would move me to prefer it is a citation that the colleagues who support it can defend without the omitted proposal being the first question the Academy gets.

responses.point: Kroll treats the lattice clock as the clearest case of better measurement opening new physics, with Katori and Ye as complete credit and the 2005 and 2012 prizes not in conflict.
responses.response: I share the conclusion but, as in round 1, not the whole premise, and the chair's question about the citation is where we differ. What has been delivered is a capability: comparisons at 1e-18, relativistic geodesy demonstrations, and constraints on constant variation and dark-matter couplings. Those searches set limits; they have not opened a new phenomenon. If we write the citation around new physics we invite exactly the objection that the payoff is prospective, and we hand the sceptics Mehlig and Olsson an easy argument. I would rather the citation say invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks and name the magic-wavelength lattice, which is where the evidence is strongest and where Pearce also wants the emphasis. I also accept Kroll's own point that his Boulder stay is relevant to how he weighs Ye, and I would support recording it, as the chair proposes, since it does not change my reading of the science.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers the fluctuation theorems (B016), accepting that clean credit is a virtue but arguing that it should be weighed against how fundamental the result is, where he thinks exact fluctuation relations score above a clock.
responses.response: I agree that clean credit alone is not sufficient and that a prize should be about something fundamental. The Jarzynski and Evans-Searles relations are exact statements and I do not dispute their depth or their experimental record. Where I disagree is on whether this decides the matter in B016's favour now. The credit is the problem: any three of Jarzynski, Evans, Crooks and Seifert omit someone whose theorem is close to the others, and Searles, Cohen and Morriss sit behind them, so the allocation would be argued as much as the physics. Mehlig himself calls that a comparable difficulty to the one in B044, and I agree. I also do not think a magic-wavelength lattice is merely instrumental: the claim that atoms in a trap can be probed with the light shift cancelled is a statement about atomic structure and light-atom interaction that had to be found. I would put B016 behind B024 and B044 on readiness, not on importance, and I am not asking Mehlig to change his scientific ranking.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, now proposes a two-part prize pairing the lattice clock (Katori, Ye) with IceCube (Halzen alone), three laureates in total, and asks that the clock citation emphasise the magic-wavelength lattice.
responses.response: I welcome the chair's emphasis on the magic-wavelength lattice and I adopt it in my citation. I cannot join the second part, though. The IceCube discovery of a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux is a real and important result and I do not question it, but a sole credit to Halzen for a collaboration of hundreds that grew out of AMANDA would be hard to defend, and the protocol does not let me add names. The chair himself lists that as the main reason B044 is his alternative, and Danielsson, Johansson and Kroll say the same. Pairing it with B024 would make the combined prize weaker than B024 alone, because the second part would be the first thing contested. If the committee wants a two-part structure I would rather see B024 paired with a part whose credit is clean, and I do not see one on this shortlist, so I hold a single-part prize.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B044 first and B024 sixth, noting overlap with the frequency-comb and ion-trap prizes and the unfinished redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I take the overlap point seriously, as I did in round 1, and I believe the answer to the chair's question is yes: magic-wavelength trapping is distinct from both earlier prizes. The 2005 prize gave a method to count optical cycles, and the 2012 prize gave control of single trapped particles. The lattice clock needs both as tools but its own idea is that a many-atom ensemble can be held with the light shift removed, so the clock transition is perturbed by the trap by almost nothing and the signal-to-noise advantage of many atoms is available. The unfinished redefinition of the second is a metrological timetable, not a doubt about the accuracy, which many laboratories have already verified. I accept her view that B044 has the broader support and I record that her argument on attribution is the same one I make; where we differ is only on which of the two weaknesses is easier to defend.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that magic-wavelength lattice trapping is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes or reads B024 as continuation of a rewarded lineage; I think it is distinct but this is a judgement.

Whether a citation for B044 limited to the prediction and the HgTe quantum-well discovery can be worded so that the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is defensible; I have not found a formulation that avoids it.

Whether Ye's platform spread and the earlier Yb and Hg lattice and Al+ ion clock work make a two-name credit contestable; I rely on recollection of priority details that are not in the supplied files.
How much weight to give the broader opening support for B044 over my own specialist judgement of B024 given my professional closeness to the clock field.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with the credited names Katori and Ye is documented in my profile: my collaborators (the Lund attosecond group including L'Huillier, ETH Zurich, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) are not among them. I remain professionally close to the optical-clock field as a theoretical atomic physicist, and I record that no relationship with Katori or Ye is documented. I have no documented tie to Kane, Mele or Molenkamp either. I support recording Johansson's recusal on B042 and Kroll's flagged Boulder stay for the final ballot.
